rewrites.title: Inducible degron depletion during the quiescent gap
rewrites.description: Tag endogenous JUN or FOS with an auxin-inducible degron (e.g., AID2), prime cells, then degrade the factor during the quiescent interval before re-challenge. If AP-1 stores the memory, degradation should erase the primed chromatin state and the faster reinduction; if the primed state survives, AP-1 is only a readout of an independent store.

rewrites.title: Two-pulse priming assay with AP-1 motif perturbation
rewrites.description: Give two stimulus pulses separated by a rest interval and measure the transcriptional response (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) in primed versus naive cells. Use CRISPR mutation or dCas9-KRAB repression of specific AP-1 motifs at candidate enhancers to test whether those sites are necessary for the enhanced second response.

rewrites.title: Single-cell multiome and live reporter tracking of heritability
rewrites.description: Combine scRNA/ATAC multiome with live imaging of an AP-1 activity reporter (a TRE-driven fluorescent protein) or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN. Follow lineages through division after a pulse to test whether the primed state passes to daughter cells and how long it lasts, and compare cell-to-cell variability and decay kinetics with non-primed controls.

rewrites.title: Stimulus pulse-chase with acute AP-1 degradation
rewrites.description: Deliver a transient stimulus (serum, TGF-beta, or a targeted inhibitor), wash out, and track AP-1 factor levels, chromatin accessibility at AP-1 motifs (ATAC-seq), and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 over days to weeks. Memory requires the open, primed state to persist after AP-1 protein has decayed; acute degradation (dTAG/auxin) of FOS/JUN at defined times after the pulse distinguishes whether AP-1 is the stored memory or only the factor that establishes the primed state.

rewrites.title: Quantitative memory transfer function from dose, duration, and rest interval
rewrites.description: Stimulate cells across a matrix of AP-1-inducing doses and durations, wash out, wait defined intervals, then apply a deliberately sub-threshold second pulse and read out target induction by scRNA-seq or a live transcriptional reporter. Fitting response amplitude and latency against first-pulse strength and rest interval yields a memory gain curve and decay half-life, the minimal quantitative signature a memory mechanism must show.

rewrites.title: Enhancer mark persistence by CUT&RUN with p300/CBP or BRD4 inhibition
rewrites.description: Map AP-1 (Fos/Jun family) occupancy, H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and Pol II pausing by CUT&RUN and ChIP-seq at multiple time points after priming, including the quiescent phase. Then inhibit p300/CBP or BRD4 during the interval to test whether retained enhancer marks are required for faster re-induction. If memory depends on these marks, blocking their maintenance should erase the primed response while leaving the first response intact.

rewrites.title: Re-stimulation kinetics of primed versus naive cells
rewrites.description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them, then give a second challenge. Use time-resolved RNA-seq or nascent transcription (PRO-seq) to compare induction speed and magnitude with naive cells, and test whether this depends on AP-1 motif-bearing enhancers. Use enhancer-motif mutants or dCas9 blocking of selected sites to test causality.

rewrites.title: Comparing AP-1 occupancy decay with accessibility decay after washout
rewrites.description: Pulse cells with a stimulus and run parallel washout time courses of AP-1 protein abundance (Halo-tag live imaging, quantitative immunoblot), AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN), and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq). Memory is supported if a class of sites retains accessibility and H3K4me1/H3K27ac for many AP-1 protein half-lives after occupancy is undetectable, with a bimodal decay-time distribution rather than one that tracks occupancy.

rewrites.title: Memory decay constant from spaced stimuli, plus ectopic motif arrays
rewrites.description: Deliver two identical stimulus pulses separated by systematically varied intervals (minutes to many days, spanning several divisions) and fit response amplitude versus inter-pulse interval to extract a memory decay constant. Test whether it matches the decay of AP-1-site accessibility rather than AP-1 protein. As a sufficiency test, insert synthetic AP-1 motif arrays at ectopic naive loci and ask whether they acquire the same memory behavior.

rewrites.title: Live-cell AP-1 imaging across repeated pulses and mitosis
rewrites.description: Image endogenously tagged FOS or JUN, or an AP-1 transcriptional reporter, in single cells over repeated pulses and across cell divisions. Quantify the dependence of response amplitude on pulse history, the decay time, and mother-daughter heritability. Add live imaging and ChIP/CUT&RUN on mitotic cells to see whether AP-1 stays on chromatin through mitosis. A history-dependent response (hysteresis) would be quantitative evidence for memory.

rewrites.title: Dilution versus turnover of the memory state in proliferating and arrested cells
rewrites.description: Compare memory persistence in proliferating versus cell-cycle-arrested cells and assay AP-1 retention on mitotic chromosomes by CUT&RUN, distinguishing stepwise loss per division from continuous chromatin turnover. Analyze which sites retain versus lose the state (motif strength, cooperating factors, CpG content, enhancer-promoter contacts) to identify determinants of durable memory.

rewrites.title: Accessibility persistence with AP-1 degradation during or after priming
rewrites.description: After a priming stimulus, use ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag for H3K27ac/H3K4me1 to identify loci that stay open once the stimulus is gone. Then acutely degrade FOS/JUN (dTAG/AID) either during priming only or after priming only, to test whether AP-1 is needed to establish or to maintain the accessible state, which separates a memory mechanism from a transient trigger.

rewrites.title: Primary versus secondary response with enhancer motif mutants
rewrites.description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to disrupt individual TRE/AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, then compare primary and secondary responses of nearby genes in wild-type and mutant clones. A memory mechanism predicts that losing a specific motif selectively abolishes the faster secondary response while leaving the first response intact.

rewrites.title: Transcriptional burst kinetics and inheritance with MS2 imaging
rewrites.description: Use MS2 live-cell imaging of an AP-1 target gene to quantify whether the remembered state is encoded in burst frequency versus amplitude, and measure sister-cell correlation of burst frequency after mitosis. Compare a second stimulus pulse with a naive first pulse: faster and larger reinduction plus inherited burst frequency is a quantitative memory signature distinguishable from residual mRNA or protein carryover.

rewrites.title: Sequential ChIP for histone marks at sites lacking AP-1
rewrites.description: Perform sequential ChIP-seq for AP-1 followed by H3K4me1, H3K27ac, or H3K4me3 at memory-associated enhancers, comparing primed cells after a rest period with naive cells. If the marks remain at sites where AP-1 is no longer bound, memory is likely carried by chromatin state rather than continued AP-1 occupancy.

rewrites.title: Chromatin persistence after AP-1 washout
rewrites.description: Pulse cells with a stimulus, wash it out, and track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for c-Jun/c-Fos) alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac over days. If accessibility and enhancer marks outlast AP-1 binding, the state is carried by chromatin rather than by the transcription factor, which is the core prediction of a memory mechanism.

rewrites.title: Washout and re-stimulation priming test
rewrites.description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF), wash out, and wait through a quiescent interval. Then re-stimulate and compare naive and primed cells by time-resolved RNA-seq and ATAC-seq. Memory is supported if primed cells show faster or stronger induction of AP-1 target genes, and the advantage disappears when the interval is extended. Persistence after stimulus removal serves as the control.

rewrites.title: Comparing FOS/JUN protein decay with persistence of accessibility
rewrites.description: Pulse-stimulate cells, wash out, and run matched time courses of FOS/JUN protein levels (quantitative immunoblot, Halo-tag pulse-chase) alongside chromatin accessibility and nucleosome positioning at AP-1 motifs (ATAC-seq plus AP-1 CUT&RUN). Memory is supported only if the accessible state at AP-1-bound enhancers outlasts the protein by many half-lives; co-decay would instead indicate ongoing signaling.

rewrites.title: Degron-based separation of AP-1 roles in establishment, maintenance, and re-stimulation
rewrites.description: Using dTAG- or auxin-tagged endogenous FOS/JUN (and a FOS-family-wide degron to address redundancy), degrade AP-1 in three nonoverlapping windows: during the priming stimulus, during the quiescent memory interval, and only at re-stimulation. Score secondary response amplitude, latency, and enhancer accessibility. This distinguishes AP-1 as the factor that establishes accessibility at latent enhancers, as a continuously required maintenance factor, or merely as a reader of a trace stored by other means (e.g., H3K4me1, CTCF loops, DNA methylation).

rewrites.title: Acute AP-1 removal at defined windows
rewrites.description: Use dTAG/AID degron alleles or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 during the initial stimulus, during the resting interval, or during restimulation. This separates whether AP-1 is needed only to establish memory or also to maintain it, and shows whether AP-1 is necessary rather than merely correlated.
